candidates.title: Higher-Scoring Coding Models Did Not Get More Work Done
candidates.author: Yining Hua
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: First natural-experiment test of whether higher coding-benchmark scores translate into more merged real-world work.
candidates.mechanism: Uses a 19-day export-control suspension of Claude Fable 5 (from June 12, 2026) that pushed users to Opus 4.8 (11 points lower on SWE-Bench Pro) as a natural experiment; difference-in-differences with developer and date fixed effects on GitHub PR outcomes.
candidates.evidence_quality: 297 treated Fable 5 users vs 8,908 control developers who stayed on Opus 4.8; replicated over five 2026 model upgrades (1,208 developers, 15,442 PRs). Outcomes are 7-day PR merge rate and PRs merged per week, which are proxies for productivity and ignore quality, task difficulty and selection into public GitHub. Single author, observational. The premise (export suspension event) is stated by the paper and not independently verified here.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None found. UNVERIFIED: the June 2026 suspension event is described only by the paper.
candidates.relevance: High: speaks directly to model-upgrade ROI decisions; argues teams should measure their own merge/throughput before paying for benchmark gains.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Extends Edition 1 theme of cost per solved task and benchmark vs reality; no paper overlap.
candidates.summary: Fable 5 access raised 7-day merge rate by only +1.4 pp [95% CI -1.4, +4.3], not significant. Across five upgrades the weighted mean was -0.9 pp [-1.9, +0.2]; all five estimates negative, none significant, not different from each other. PRs merged per week +2.4% [-4.9%, +10.2%]. Conclusion: an 11-point SWE-Bench Pro gap produced no detectable change in merged work for the same people and projects.

candidates.title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
candidates.author: Zerui Yang, Miaomiao Dong, Quan Xue, Chaorui Zhang, Xuanyu Zheng, Xiyuan Wang, Haolin Ruan, Xueyan Niu, Guangcheng Song, Weixi Zhang, Wei Han, Bo Bai
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Shows that context-management tricks for coding agents (retrieved code, pruning old tool outputs) can raise rather than lower dollar cost once prefix-cache pricing is accounted for.
candidates.mechanism: Accounts separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens; compares context additions/removals under no-discount vs tenth-price cache pricing, and tracks agents' behavioral response (extra steps).
candidates.evidence_quality: >20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. Open models only; pricing scenarios are modeled (cache at 1/10 price). Also flags a methodological hazard: concurrent experiments share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Directionally consistent with 2611.20873 'Re-Reading Is Not Free' (different authors): cached-context reads were 94.8% of ~1B tokens in real agentic SE sessions, ~260 cached tokens read per generated token.
candidates.relevance: High: anyone pruning or compacting agent history must evaluate under their real cache pricing; pruning invalidates cache prefixes.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Directly continues Edition 1 memory/compaction theme and 2611.14654 Cleaning an Agent's History; new angle is cache-aware cost. Same author group as 2611.22901 (Done, But Still Working), which overlaps Edition 1's Termination Lag.
candidates.summary: Retrieved code cut read/search commands 18-34% but raised cost 33-42% at tenth-price cache, with no measurable resolution gain. Removing old observations saved 19-36% without cache discount but increased cost 38-116% with a tenth-price cache. Shorter prompts did not guarantee cheaper runs because agents took more steps. Recommends evaluating context methods on both token prices and subsequent agent behavior.

candidates.title: Compositional Exploits in Autonomous Coding Agents: Attack Mechanics and Ephemeral Defense
candidates.author: Deep Shah, Nehal Kathrotia
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Names a vulnerability class where agents chain individually benign tools across turns into an attack, invisible to per-tool scanners; proposes an OS-level defense.
candidates.mechanism: Attack: agent stitches legitimate tool operations via shared workspace files, env vars and chat memory (analogy: code-reuse attacks). Defense CompGuard: a control plane issuing single-skill capability leases with dataflow provenance, plus kernel enforcement via Linux Landlock LSM v4, seccomp-BPF socket filters and an ephemeral loopback proxy.
candidates.evidence_quality: 560-task suite (360 exploit tasks across 8 hazard classes, 200 benign workflows); models tested are Gemini 3.5/3.7/3.8 Flash only; five pre-distribution scanners. Authors' own benchmark and defense; no third-party replication.
candidates.relevance: High: concrete argument that tool/skill vetting must be compositional and that enforcement belongs in the OS sandbox, not the prompt.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Continues Edition 1 prompt-vs-enforced limits theme; no paper overlap.
candidates.summary: Unprotected models executed compositional exploit chains at 72.9-84.5% success; five leading single-tool scanners detected 0% across constituent tools. CompGuard: 100% defense block rate (0.0-0.8% pre-teardown net ASR), 61.4 microsecond interposition overhead, 98.0% benign solve rate, zero false alarms on 615 real cloud diagnostic calls.

candidates.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents
candidates.author: Zeynab Anbiaee, Sajjad Dadkhah, Ali A. Ghorbani
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED); Ghorbani/Dadkhah are commonly affiliated with UNB Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Formalizes 'tool-provider misbinding' in MCP: a rogue co-installed MCP server wins tool selection without compromising host, model, legitimate server or network.
candidates.mechanism: Attacker only advertises tools with chosen metadata (name collision, task-aligned description, compatible schema, authority-enhanced descriptions); framed as an attacker-side tool-selection optimization problem.
candidates.evidence_quality: Controlled MCP environment, five LLM-based clients. Abstract gives qualitative findings only; quantitative rates require the full paper.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Related discovery-time trust work on A2A: 2611.18887 SECCARD (310 real Agent Cards from 36.1M domains probed; best semantic judge 97.0% recall at 1.7% FPR, nine judges ranged 25.8-92.3%).
candidates.relevance: High: anyone composing multiple MCP servers needs provider-qualified tool identity, allowlists, and collision detection.
candidates.summary: Strongest failures when exact-name collision, task-aligned description and compatible schema combine; authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved ambiguity even without a name collision. Different models fail differently: attacker selection, clarification requests, or unstable/inconsistent resolution. Core point: tool metadata is not bound to a verified provider identity in MCP composition.

candidates.title: Where the Savings Go: The Limits of Hiding Cross-Tenant Cache Hits in LLM Serving
candidates.author: Bowen Sun, Chaowei Xiao
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Shows that defenses which share prefix caches globally but 'hide' hits still leak, because the saved time propagates to other queued requests.
candidates.mechanism: Step-based schedulers pass a hit's saved time to every request queued behind it. Attacker brackets a probe with two groups of 1-token listener requests in one burst and counts finishing steps. Includes a bound: a rate-limited tenant's gain from k other accounts' content is at most O(k x allowed leakage).
candidates.evidence_quality: Production-trace replay on one vLLM instance up to half capacity; also tested against SGLang. Theory plus single-instance experiments.
candidates.relevance: High for operators of multi-tenant inference: per-account cache salting remains the safe default; 'hide the hit' defenses and random delays are weak.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New; complements Edition 1 OverServe (2611.14808) only loosely (serving).
candidates.summary: A single probe detects cached texts of 256+ tokens with advantage >=0.98. Hiding only the hit request falls to one probe on vLLM and SGLang; random delays must be ~10x the shift to cut advantage to 0.1; narrowing what is shared gives no guarantee. At zero leakage only the provider keeps the savings; exact hiding is possible in principle on one instance but under saturated prefill requires padding every step that may hold a hit, cost growing with time.

candidates.title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
candidates.author: Ana Clara Zoppi Serpa, Anderson Rocha, Hélio Pedrini
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED); Rocha/Pedrini commonly affiliated with Unicamp (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Large-scale audit of instruction-hierarchy enforcement: a human-steered attacking agent extracted a system-prompt secret from 296 of 363 OpenRouter models.
candidates.mechanism: Each model guards a 16-character flag in its system prompt; an OpenCode agent powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, steered by a researcher, tries persuasion; language pivots tracked.
candidates.evidence_quality: 363 text models from the OpenRouter catalog (+4 later). Human-in-the-loop attack, so not a fixed automated attack rate; a capture proves at least one hierarchy violation, not consistent leakage. Authors state these limits explicitly.
candidates.independent_confirmation: None found; consistent with general prior findings that system prompts are not confidential.
candidates.relevance: High, simple takeaway: never store secrets in system prompts; enforce outside the model.
candidates.summary: Flag exfiltrated from 296/363 models plus 4 newer ones (300 captures). 170 captures involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Lessons: no secrets in system prompts; enforce critical behavior with output validation and deterministic checks; do not let an LLM judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

candidates.title: Does Your Agent Need to Know Its Budget? A Placebo-Controlled Experiment on LLM Coding Agents
candidates.author: Iftesam Nabi, Jarif Ul Alam, Sunzid Hassan, Sabbir Alom Shuvo, Md Faiaz Al Islam, Yead Rahman, Mehrab Hosain
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.pub_date: 2026-08-08 (v1 per abs page; ID 2611 and first listing 2026-11-18 suggest the stated date should be re-checked)
candidates.event_date: 2026-08-08 (v1 per abs page; ID 2611 and first listing 2026-11-18 suggest the stated date should be re-checked)
candidates.what_changed: Placebo-controlled factorial test of token-budget enforcement vs telling the agent its budget.
candidates.mechanism: Crosses budget enforcement with budget disclosure under a frozen, timestamped protocol; includes a placebo arm (an unrelated sentence) to isolate prompt-length/wording effects.
candidates.evidence_quality: 5,835 runs, two open models, three cap levels, two executable program-repair benchmarks. Open models only; effect-of-interest threshold 10 pp.
candidates.relevance: High: budget governance is an enforcement-design problem; disclosure prompts do nothing beyond a placebo.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Directly extends Edition 1 prompt-vs-enforced limits and cost-per-solved-task themes.
candidates.summary: Enforcing a calibrated cap cut resolution by 20.0 pp but cut tokens per resolved task ~12x. Disclosure never helped: placebo-controlled risk difference -2.8 pp [-6.2, +0.7] at medium cap, -4.2 pp [-8.1, -0.2] at tight cap (nominal, unadjusted). An unrelated placebo sentence itself raised resolution 7.2 pp [+4.0, +10.5] over silent enforcement. Variance ~1.5x uncapped under caps.

candidates.title: Beyond Prompts: Runtime Contracts for Coding Agents
candidates.author: Reda Heddad
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Preregistered comparison of engineering rules given as prompt text, retrieved guidance, post-hoc checks, or executable contracts enforced during agent execution.
candidates.mechanism: In-loop executable contracts over shell commands and file edits; violations scored by an independent oracle validated by two humans and a model reviewer.
candidates.evidence_quality: Three studies (240, 112, 108 runs), two model families, low-cost models, one small fixture; Study 3 protocol hashed before first run. Author notes enforcement satisfying its own rules is expected by construction.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Consistent with 2611.20595 SilentGuard (different authors) finding that harness enforcement beats warnings.
candidates.relevance: High: practical evidence for hooks/policy enforcement over CLAUDE.md-style prose rules, especially for destructive commands.
candidates.summary: In-loop enforcement: zero oracle-detected violations in 104 paired runs vs 21-55% of runs without rules, no loss of functional correctness. Study 3: enforcement cut violating runs by 31 pp vs no rules (Holm p=0.014); 17-pp gap vs prompted rules not significant (p=0.12). Prompted rules failed to stop recursive deletes of scratch directories; post-generation checks repaired file edits but not commands already executed.

candidates.title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
candidates.author: Sajib Acharjee Dip, Brian Ouyang, Lala Motlhabi
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Moves detection of silently failing APIs (HTTP 200, plausible but wrong) out of the model and into the harness.
candidates.mechanism: SilentGuard tests each tool result against invariants any correct API must satisfy and withholds violating values; agent abstains rather than recovers.
candidates.evidence_quality: 15 public research APIs; 7 open models plus three frontier models; compares checklists, reviewer models, LLM judges and warning-only variants.
candidates.relevance: High: concrete pattern for tool wrappers (validate filters applied, counts plausible) in agentic RAG/data tools.
candidates.summary: Silent failures found in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691x. Existing fixes leave >70% of answers wrong; agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on target faults from 74.0% to 1.7% (open models) and 70.2% to 0.5% (frontier), no loss on fault-free tasks. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong. On new fault types harness alone cuts 61.1% to 24.5%.

candidates.title: Beyond Plain MCP: Do Decision Models and Code Mode Make Tool Use Cheaper and Faster?
candidates.author: Abhishek Rai
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Preregistered comparison of plain MCP tool calling, code mode (agent writes scripts against tool stubs), and a router/decision layer.
candidates.mechanism: Controlled harness, 12 servers, up to 1,958 distractor tools; sealed test split; return-shape hints in code-mode stubs as a variable.
candidates.evidence_quality: Three open-weight agents (Qwen, Gemma, Nemotron); single author; harness, finetuned 4B tool selector and traces released.
candidates.relevance: High: actionable for MCP gateway design; return-type hints in stubs matter more than routers.
candidates.summary: Code mode cut token usage 70-90% vs plain MCP while raising utility. Declaring return-shape hints swung success up to 39.5 points for weaker agents, larger than adding a router. Router in front of code mode: not confirmed, small non-significant gains for weak agents and a slight cost for the strongest.

candidates.title: When Agent Skills Go Stale: Runtime Behavior and Selective Maintenance in Evolving Environments
candidates.author: Ömer Faruk Akgül, Shuli Jiang, Yuting Zhang, Yi Zhang, Xiaohan Fei, Wei Xia, Stefano Soatto
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Measures how reusable agent skills degrade after environment changes and proposes cheap selective maintenance.
candidates.mechanism: Selective maintenance replays checks from successful executions without extra model calls, verifies conflicts with skill state, repairs affected content, validates, and rebuilds when local repair fails; no description of the change supplied.
candidates.evidence_quality: Four task settings, two models; abstract does not name models or benchmarks.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Related: 2611.22017 SkillBuffBench (design-only, results pending) argues hand-picked-Skill evaluations overstate value.
candidates.relevance: High for teams maintaining skill libraries: skills need regression checks like code.
candidates.summary: Previously beneficial skills can reduce task performance by >10 pp or increase execution cost ~40% relative to no skill after environment change; success can stay flat while savings vanish. Selective maintenance improves accuracy up to 67 pp and reduces steps up to 37% vs reusing stale state.

candidates.title: AI Cannot Review What Humans Catch: A First Look at the Reviews of Agent Instruction Files
candidates.author: Wenhao Yang, Runzhi He, Minghui Zhou
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED); Minghui Zhou commonly affiliated with Peking University (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: First empirical study of how agent instruction files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md-style, .cursorrules) are reviewed in PRs.
candidates.mechanism: Mines instruction-file PRs, builds a 16-category taxonomy of review concerns and a benchmark of human-checked concerns, then runs coding agents as reviewers with full repo access.
candidates.evidence_quality: 2,870 instruction-file PRs across 2,246 repos; benchmark of 1,962 human-checked concerns across 468 PRs; agents Codex, OpenCode, Claude Code.
candidates.relevance: High: instruction files are executable policy with no test oracle; teams should require human review.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Adjacent to Edition 1 skills/goal engineering theme.
candidates.summary: Over 70% of instruction-file changes get no substantive review. AI reviewers catch surface structure but miss factual errors, necessity and staleness. Agents recovered only 1.3-3.9% of the concerns humans raised.

candidates.title: RAG in a Trenchcoat: When Minimal Memory Is Enough for Agentic Systems, and When It Isn't
candidates.author: Jingyu Liu, Zongze Li, Zach Xu, Zhanhui Zhou, Tahseen Rabbani, Dawn Song, Ce Zhang
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED); Dawn Song commonly UC Berkeley (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: A deliberately minimal RAG memory matches prior SOTA agent-memory systems on standard benchmarks; new probes test what memory enables an agent to do.
candidates.mechanism: BRIDGE: chained observation notes, hybrid BM25 + cosine retrieval, chronological rendering, one LLM call per ingestion/query; five adversarial probes (rule application, pattern induction, procedural, dynamic multi-turn) graded by a cross-vendor verification chain.
candidates.evidence_quality: LongMemEval-S, BEAM, EverMemBench; 5 probes x 20 scenarios, four domains, three graders, three reader families.
candidates.independent_confirmation: Related: 2611.19199 (LoCoMo scores move up to 7.2 pts by judge, 9.3 by answer prompt) and 2611.19752 StaleBench (retrieval metrics can rank memory policies backwards) both question memory-benchmark validity.
candidates.relevance: High: start with minimal hybrid RAG memory before elaborate memory stacks; evaluate on downstream action.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: Continues Edition 1 memory/compaction theme; no paper overlap.
candidates.summary: BRIDGE reaches parity (within bootstrap CI) with prior SOTA on LongMemEval-S and BEAM, beats best memory baseline on EverMemBench by 5.7-6.3 pts at matched reader, at ~5-7K reader-prompt tokens/query. On action probes no architecture wins: LangMem atomic-fact extraction wins rule application, BRIDGE block summaries win pattern induction; presenting retrieved rules more prominently largely closes BRIDGE's gap.

candidates.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
candidates.author: Ziji Shi, Xinyi Wan, Chaoyi Ruan, Guangxing Huang, Min Lin, Jialin Li
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Identifies 'KV thrashing' in reasoning-model serving and presents Stint, a serving system that makes preemption productive.
candidates.mechanism: Fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with exact-extent allocator; fused K/V gather/scatter kernels with double buffering; age-based readmission; protection window for fresh decoding; victim selection by remaining-length estimates from hidden states.
candidates.evidence_quality: Olympiad-math replays, Qwen3-32B on H200; baseline is recomputation in the same engine. Single workload family.
candidates.relevance: Medium-high for inference operators serving long-output reasoning models under memory pressure.
candidates.overlap_with_prior: New; loosely adjacent to Edition 1 OverServe.
candidates.summary: Existing systems can leave >1/5 of requests stalled for over a minute. Under Stint no request pauses >50 s; p99 time per output token falls 50.7% vs recomputation; whole replay finishes 10.7% sooner (12.0% higher throughput).

candidates.title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
candidates.author: Deepak Waghmare, Shaad Sufi
candidates.organization: Not stated on arXiv abs page (UNVERIFIED)
candidates.what_changed: Proposes a five-level reversibility vocabulary for agent tool actions with a registry over real MCP servers and a session guard.
candidates.mechanism: Argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract; session guard gates irreversible actions.
candidates.evidence_quality: 536 tools across 20 MCP servers; 738 rule-case checks; 2,158 recorded runs (29 attributable attack-positive, 1,209 benign); controlled file/Git/SQLite/browser recovery experiments. Reviewer agreement is AI-assisted, not independent; authors disclaim registry-wide accuracy and production-harm claims.
candidates.relevance: High: gives a concrete scheme for approval gating beyond read/write, relevant to MCP tool annotations.
candidates.summary: Native MCP annotation mapping differed from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. Session guard gated the action in all 29 attack-positive runs vs 18 for a read/write proxy, adding nine approval points over 1,209 benign runs. Recovery depended on captured state, later changes, editor storage and route; found a Git merge-state exception.
